lesson.title: Letting the Bass Through: How Low-Pass Filters Work
lesson.summary: A low-pass filter passes frequencies below its cutoff frequency largely unattenuated and increasingly suppresses frequencies above it, the most common filter shape in circuits from audio tone controls to power supply smoothing.
lesson.body:
A low-pass filter is the simplest member of the family introduced in Filter: its passband sits at low frequencies, from DC up to a cutoff frequency, and its stopband sits above that cutoff. The cutoff frequency, covered in Cutoff Frequency, is conventionally the point where output power has dropped to half its passband value, equivalently where output voltage amplitude has dropped to 1/√2, about 0.707, of the input, a drop of about 3 dB.

The classic way to build one uses a single resistor and capacitor arranged as a voltage divider, with the resistor in series with the signal and the capacitor connected from the output node to ground. At low frequencies the capacitor's reactance 1/(ωC) is large compared with R, so almost none of the divider's voltage drop happens across R and almost all of it appears across C, meaning the output tracks the input closely. At high frequencies the capacitor's reactance shrinks toward zero, so it behaves increasingly like a short to ground, pulling the output down toward zero regardless of what the input is doing. That single frequency-dependent component is the entire mechanism of the filter.

The transfer function magnitude for this RC divider is |H(f)| = 1/√(1 + (f/fc)²), where fc = 1/(2πRC). This formula gives |H| close to 1, essentially no attenuation, when f is much smaller than fc, and |H| shrinking roughly in proportion to fc/f once f is well above fc.

Take R = 1 kΩ and C = 100 nF. The product RC = 1000 times 100 times 10 to the minus 9, which is 1 times 10 to the minus 4 seconds. The cutoff frequency is fc = 1/(2π times 1 times 10 to the minus 4), about 1591 Hz, roughly 1.59 kHz. Check the cutoff definition directly: at f = fc, |H| = 1/√(1+1) = 1/√2, about 0.707, and in decibels, 20 log10(0.707) is about minus 3.0 dB, confirming that fc really is the minus 3 dB point.

Because this filter has only one reactive element, it belongs to the family covered in First-Order Filter, and its attenuation beyond cutoff grows at a fixed rate of 20 dB per decade, the subject of Roll-Off Rate. You will meet this exact RC topology again, with a fresh set of component values, in RC Low-Pass Filter.
